item.title: U.S. futures mostly higher with the Fed’s Warsh touting AI
item.description: U.S. futures are mostly higher as U.S. Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh touts the benefits of artificial intelligence, a sector that has been hammered this week by concerns over the rising costs ...
item.dc:creator: The Associated Press
item.content:encoded: U.S. futures are mostly higher as U.S. Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh touts the benefits of artificial intelligence, a sector that has been hammered this week by concerns over the rising costs of borrowing money. Futures for the S&P 500 gained 0.2 per cent on Friday, while those for the Dow Jones Industrial Average climbed 0.4 per cent. Nasdaq futures dipped 0.1 per cent. Warsh said Friday at the IMF and World Bank gathering in Bangkok that AI could have a positive impact on the global economy. “I’d say the advent of this new technology is probably the most consequential change to the U.S. and the global economy in my lifetime,” Warsh said. “There really is, I think, a huge benefit to the global economy, the U.S. economy, over the horizon.” AI and chip stocks were choppy before the market opened Friday. Nvidia was flat after closing down 1.8 per cent on Thursday, and shares are down more than five per cent this week. Broadcom’s stock declined 0.7 per cent before the market open, while those for Advanced Micro Devices fell 1.8 per cent. Shares of Tesla climbed more than three per cent after the electric vehicle maker unveiled its Roadster sports car that will go into production in two years. Netflix’s stock fell more than three per cent after the company announced that Chief Content Officer Bela Bajaria will be replaced by Peter Rice. The news comes just days after Netflix said that it plans to lay off about six per cent of its workforce, amounting to nearly 1,000 positions. Oil prices are still elevated as the global oil supply remains under pressure without a deal between the U.S. and Iran to end the Iran war. Brent crude, the international standard, rose 0.3 per cent to US$106.27 per barrel. That is still high compared with around $72 a barrel in late February before the start of the war. Brent climbed into triple digits last month, the first time since July. Benchmark U.S. crude edged 0.2 per cent lower to $97.77 per barrel. The national average for gasoline is at $4.33 a gallon on Friday, according to AAA. While that’s lower than the $4.37 a gallon that it averaged last month, it’s sharply higher than the $3.06 a gallon from a year ago. Oil remains well-supported as uncertainties surrounding the situation in the Middle East and concerns over oil flows in the Strait of Hormuz had the market “pricing in a significant risk premium,” ING commodities strategists Warren Patterson and Ewa Manthey wrote in a commentary Friday. In Europe, Britain’s FTSE 100 declined slightly to 10,837.99. France’s CAC 40 gained 0.4 per cent to 7,966.11, while Germany’s DAX rose one per cent to 25,645.64. Asian markets were higher. The U.S. dollar rose to 158.02 Japanese yen from 158 yen. The euro was trading at $1.1256, up from $1.1220. By Chan Ho-him and Michelle Chapman

item.title: Canadian steelmakers offset some U.S. tariff pain with domestic demand
item.description: Canada’s steel industry, among the sectors hit first and hardest by U.S. President Donald Trump’s tariffs, is starting to turn a corner thanks to an uptick in mining, energy and AI data centre ...
item.dc:creator: Reuters Staff
item.content:encoded: TORONTO -- Canada’s steel industry, among the sectors hit first and hardest by U.S. President Donald Trump’s tariffs, is starting to turn a corner thanks to an uptick in mining, energy and AI data centre projects as well as government support, although the impact has not been even across the country. While Canada is a small producer globally and steel contributes less than 1 per cent to national GDP, it is one sector in which Prime Minister Mark Carney’s efforts to make Canada’s economy less reliant on the United States appear to be having some success, albeit with a heavy dose of government intervention. Steel companies have been diversifying away from the U.S. and focusing on domestic demand since Trump increased tariffs on imported steel from 25 per cent to 50 per cent in June 2025, steelmakers, analysts and union representatives said. Canada used to send around 90 per cent of its steel exports to the U.S., but shipments plummeted by 60 per cent in 2025, according to the Canadian Steel Producers Association. Hundreds of steelworkers have been laid off. But the share of steel used in Canada that was produced domestically rose to 51 per cent in 2025, up from 41 per cent in 2024, according to United Steelworkers, the sector’s main labor union. The import share declined from 59 per cent to 49 per cent. USW calculated the data based on World Steel Data and Canada’s imported steel data, said Guio Jacinto, an economic researcher for the union. The green shoots are mostly appearing in western Canada, where some large industrial projects including a 1.2 gigawatt data centre in Saskatchewan are under construction. Carney said a new oil pipeline to the Pacific Coast would also boost demand for steel. Canadian steel demand is estimated to have grown around 2.7 per cent in 2025 and is projected to increase by about 0.9 per cent in 2026, according to an OECD report published in July. “What we are seeing right now is that more Canadian companies are competing for domestic market, which means there is less space for steelmakers from outside,” said David Fritz of Alberta-based Supreme Steel, which manufactures fabricated steel. “I feel optimistic for the outlook of fabricated steel market in Canada, there are enough projects in pipeline to support this industry,” Fritz added. Government intervention At a time of excess global capacity, Canadian steel would struggle to compete with lower-cost producers in China and South Korea without import quotas. Canada produces around 13 million tonnes of primary steel annually. In May, the federal government announced $1 billion (US$700 million) in loans to the steel, aluminum and copper industries as working capital funding to get through the impact of U.S. tariffs. The government extended a cap on foreign steel coming into the country, known as tariff rate quota, to address the issue of foreign steel dumping. Canada’s adaptation to Trump’s tariffs has been closely watched internationally, as Carney is one of the few global leaders to retaliate against U.S. tariffs despite his country’s overwhelming economic dependence on the U.S.. The prime minister also threatened legal action against U.S. steel producer Cleveland-Cliffs over plans to cut hundreds of jobs at its Hamilton, Ont., facility. Cleveland-Cliffs, which acquired Canada’s Stelco in 2024, said in its second-quarter earnings there was steep international competition for the galvanized steel produced at the Hamilton plant, but the market for its specific hot-rolled steel produced elsewhere in Canada contributed to improved guidance for the second half of 2026. Cleveland-Cliffs will report quarterly results on October 19, potentially giving a clearer picture of the future of its Canadian operations. Domestic market pivot Luxembourg-headquartered Tenaris, which manufactures steel pipes for energy companies at its Sault Ste Marie, Ontario, facility, said it recently invested $306 million to expand production of its Canadian-made products for Canadian customers. “This strengthens Tenaris’s commitment to produce in Canada what Canada’s oil and gas industry needs. As a result, the company’s exposure to the United States tariffs is limited,” said Martín Castro, president of Tenaris in Canada, in an email. The largest Canadian steel producer, Algoma, said in December it would lay off 1,000 workers in Ontario – accounting for nearly all of the sector layoffs nationally since tariffs were imposed. But the company’s CEO recently touted the strengthening domestic market, citing growing infrastructure, construction and defense demand for its discrete steel plate. “While the 50 per cent U.S. Section 232 tariffs continue to effectively foreclose our traditional access to the U.S. market, our pivot to a Canada-centric, plate-first strategy is working,” CEO Rajat Marwah said on an earnings call in July. Marty Warren, head of the Canadian branch of the USW, said there has been a turnaround in the industry but a bigger revival would require replacing even more imported steel with domestic production. The union also wants Canada to tighten the quota on imported steel and put tariffs on steel used in the U.S. auto and aviation industries, which are currently exempt from broader retaliatory tariffs by Canada. Canada’s finance ministry said the steel sector remained exposed to tariffs and the government was encouraging investment through a number of policies, such as buying Canadian steel for infrastructure projects. “This is evidenced by the domestic demand cycle we are enabling through the Buy Canadian policy and more generally the government’s growth agenda which will require Canadian steel and workers,” the ministry said in an emailed statement. Divya Rajagopal in Toronto, additional reporting by Promit Mukherjee; Editing by Caroline Stauffer and Nia Williams, Reuters

item.title: Bank of Canada set for pair of important data drops ahead of 'live' rate decision
item.description: The Bank of Canada will get a raft of fresh data to start next week as it weighs what could be a pivotal interest rate decision at the end of the month.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: OTTAWA — The Bank of Canada will get a raft of fresh data to start next week as it weighs what could be a pivotal interest rate decision at the end of the month. Statistics Canada is set to release its September inflation data on Monday, giving the central bank a look at how energy price pressures are influencing other parts of the consumer basket. RBC assistant chief economist Nathan Janzen says he expects the annual rate of inflation held steady around three per cent last month, mostly because of persistently high gasoline prices. Janzen says the Bank of Canada’s upcoming decision on Oct. 28 will be a “live” meeting, where the door is open for the central bank to raise its policy rate, but a hike is not his base case scenario. Even if the September price data shows signs inflationary pressures are spreading past the gas pumps, Janzen says the central bank will be weighing that against signs of softness in the labour market and wider economy. The Bank of Canada will also release its own quarterly surveys of businesses and consumers on Monday, which can give the bank a better sense of whether firms are planning to pass their own rising costs on to consumers. “Higher energy prices — all else equal — would mean broader inflation pressures would be expected to rise in the future. But if the economy is getting weaker, then there are some offsetting disinflationary forces there as well,” Janzen says. “It puts (the Bank of Canada) still in a wait-and-see mode — very, very data dependent.” This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 16, 2026. Craig Lord, The Canadian Press

item.title: 8 must-own stocks for the rest of 2026: Jon Erlichman
item.description: In the latest episode of Ticker Take, I spoke with Pettit, chief investment strategist at Roundhill Investments, who returned to the show with his investment ideas for the rest of the year. Pettit has ...
item.content:encoded:
Some investors think it’s time to move away from big tech. Drew Pettit says that could be a dangerous mistake.

His bullish case comes down to three words: revisions, revisions, revisions. In the latest episode of Ticker Take , I spoke with Pettit, chief investment strategist at Roundhill Investments, who returned to the show with his investment ideas for the rest of the year. Pettit has a strong track record, having joined us late last year with his 2026 picks, which included standout names such as Nvidia, CrowdStrike and Teradyne. His framework starts with the estimates Wall Street uses to value stocks. He said in our interview that analysts have been consistently too low on profits, and they keep having to move their numbers higher. That holds even in a messy macro environment, and Pettit says it is the main reason big tech keeps surprising people who wrote it off. It also changes how you read valuation. While many investors look at the price-to-earnings ratio, Pettit says that misses the point if earnings keep rising. He prefers to compare the price of a stock to the company’s growth, known as the PEG ratio. On that measure, he says, the Magnificent Seven and other big cap tech stocks are not that expensive and look cheaper than small caps because they have growth that smaller companies don’t yet have. With that in mind, he highlighted eight names he likes heading into the final stretch of 2026. We also included some of the analyst recommendations, as measured by Bloomberg. As always, this is not financial advice. Meta Platforms ( META ) More than 90 per cent of the 79 analysts covering it recommend buying. Pettit says Meta is a stock people keep writing off, and it keeps surprising to the upside, most recently with the launch of its Muse AI model. He notes that estimates for 2027 and 2028 are up 10 to 20 per cent from the start of the year, and he says its PEG ratio is more attractive than the S&P 500. Alphabet ( GOOGL ) Roughly 90 per cent of the 71 analysts covering it recommend buying. Pettit puts it in the same revisions camp as Meta, with analysts raising their earnings expectations in the out years. He points to the launch of Gemini 4, which got great reviews. Micron Technology ( MU ) Again, more than 90 per cent of the 62 analysts covering it recommend buying. Memory has a reputation as a boom-and-bust business, but Pettit says this time it doesn’t feel that way. The computing power needed to run AI models keeps rising, and Wall Street has been raising its margin forecasts, which he says suggests profits will be more stable than in past cycles. Samsung Electronics All 44 analysts covering it recommend buying, and none have a sell. It trades in South Korea, which makes it harder for most investors to buy directly, making it a commonly sought after name in ETFs. Pettit says that Micron has much better margins, but he expects that gap to close significantly over the next few years. CrowdStrike ( CRWD ) Nearly three-quarters of the 62 analysts covering it recommend buying, even after the stock’s big move since Pettit first flagged it. Software has been a tough place to pick stocks because of fears of AI disruption, but he says cybersecurity is the exception. More AI agents and more data mean more to defend. Snowflake ( SNOW ) Currently, just under 90 per cent of the 57 analysts covering it recommend buying. Pettit gives three reasons for why he likes it: estimates are rising, AI may help drive more business for the company rather than disrupt it and the stock has very low correlation to the broader market and to semiconductors. In his view, that can help diversify your portfolio. Lumentum ( LITE ) Like Snowflake, nearly 90 per cent of the 35 analysts covering it recommend buying. The company makes optical components that move data inside AI data centres. Pettit says the stock has pulled back and been more volatile than it should be, but the story hasn’t changed. Estimates are still rising, growth is still good, and he calls it a tactical buying opportunity. Kirby ( KEX ) Kirby is the surprise pick on the list. All seven analysts who cover it recommend buying, though that is a small group. Kirby falls into a category known as HALO, which stands for hard asset, low obsolescence. These are viewed as physical businesses AI can’t easily disrupt. In Kirby’s case, Pettit says that means moving chemicals and oil products by water. The Ticker Take Pettit’s list is a bet that the market is still underestimating how much profit big tech can generate. Seven of the eight names are tied to the AI trade in some way, and the eighth is there to hedge against it. That also means the list is not for everyone. If revisions stop moving up, the argument weakens quickly, and several of these stocks have already had big runs. For investors who share his view, though, it is a useful reminder that the stocks some people think have stalled out may be the ones where analysts are still catching up. Jon Erlichman is a BNN Bloomberg contributor and the host of Ticker Take on YouTube .
